newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Rabobank mulls growth in booming Asian commodities.
newsitem.headline: Rabobank mulls growth in booming Asian commodities.

text.p: Dutch cooperative Rabobank is enjoying strong revenue growth in a booming Southeast Asian commodities market and sees the potential for expansion into derivatives trade, officials said on Friday.

Yong Meng, head of trade and commodity finance at Rabobank's Singapore office, told Reuters in an interview that the bank had experienced near double-digit revenue growth in commodity financing in the region.
He added Rabobobank would probably move into futures trading, for hedging purposes, perhaps in two to three years time. "It will definitely come," he said.

Cheam Hing Lee, senior manager for trade and commodity finance at Rabobank, Singapore, said the growth in commodities trade in Southeast Asia was particularly strong in the vegetable oils and animal feedstuffs sectors.

This business has been driven by the flow of palm oil from the expanding production in Malaysia and Indonesia to the West, China and the Indian subcontinent and the reverse movement of corn and soymeal to feed the region's growing poultry industry.

He estimated that Rabobank had roughly a 60 percent share of the agricultural commodities trade finance market in Southeast Asia where prices of basic products such as palm oil had doubled in the past five years, since the "crash of 1989".
Yong said Rabobank's policy of concentrating 50 percent of its business in food and agricultural commodities is leading the bank towards trading in over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives.
"It (OTC commodities derivatives trading) has been taken up at the highest level...it's logical," Yong said.
The size and quality of Rabobank's customers are also increasing as niche players grow in markets such as rice and Asian trading companies themselves become more sophisticated.

"Five years ago the Indian soymeal industry would only sell FAS (free alongside ship), but now the whole economy is much more liberalised and we've seen a lot of Indian trading companies moving into Singapore," Cheam said.
He added that the first direct trade between an Indian soymeal producer and an Indonesian buyer had recently been done.
Whereas there was a handful of Indian traders involved in buying green beans and pulses in Burma four years ago now "there are hundreds", Cheam added.

The growth in commodity finance business had attracted other banks into the sector, but it continued to be dominated by Dutch companies such as MeesPierson and ING Bank and French banks like Societe Generale.

Rabobank recently arranged a novel trade finance facility, the first of its kind in Singapore, with Indonesian rubber company Lewis & Peat (Rubber) Holdings Pte Ltd, part of PT Bakrie Sumatra Plantation.
This involved Rabobank as the sole financier in a US$150 million syndicated trade finance facility, which is a hybrid combining trade financing and syndication.

Rabobank said it would fund and control all future transactions for Lewis & Peat as well as finance its futures contracts. Yong said Rabobank had three other similar deals in the pipeline, but declined to elaborate further.
